What are you scripting in? Python has an awesome package called Requests that makes REST calls a breeze. My comment history is beginning to look like I wrote the package or something...I LOVE Requests, I can't help it. It's so easy.

import requests

url = 'your url here'
header = { 'apitoken' : 'your api token here','maybesomethingelseintheheader' : 'whatever the value is' }

r = requests.get(url,headers=header)
r.status() // this gives you the status code - 200 is good!
r.text // this dumps all of the return data
r.json() // this automatically decodes the json response

I wouldn't keep any bitcoins in Circle or Coinbase unless I'm about to buy them or use them. If something goes wrong on their end, you can lose everything. The moment I buy bitcoins from Circle or Coinbase, I immediately transfer the coins to a local wallet with addresses that only I know the private keys to.

What's important is owning the private keys to your addresses. If you don't own those keys (or if someone else has access to those keys) you don't control those bitcoins.

You're asking the right questions!

There's different levels of security for online wallets. Some factors are whether they offer Two Factor Authentication, access to private keys, and multisig. It depends on how 'hardcore' you want to get with being in control of your own security. Circle requires 2FA, so you're covered there. They don't give you access to the private keys, so that means they could decide to take away your bitcoins. Chances of that happening are fairly low since they have a reputation to think of, but they may ask you for some personal info to verify your identity at some point, so be prepared for that.

Circle is pretty okay for a primary wallet if you just want a simple and safe way to send/receive bitcoin and convert to/from your bank account. Their mobile app is decent too, but their overall platform is incredibly basic. The only thing I'd caution against is storing large amounts of bitcoin at Circle (or Coinbase or any other centralized wallet). In that case, you would really want to learn more about properly securing your own coins using multisig and/or a hardware wallet like Trezor or Ledger. If you want complete control of your own coin, but not necessarily for long-term investment purposes, then Breadwallet is an excellent option.

I'd say no. Keep that wallet to yourself. Things change obviously but Dogewallet is a good example of what can happen. You are placing a lot of trust in infrastructure you don't necessarily know a lot about. I seem to remember in Dogewallets case hackers gained access to the back end infrastructure, took what they wanted and then deleted all the Virtual Machines.

I guess the question comes up what to do in your situation though. It is not only wise to have a local wallet but it's good it back that wallet up. I'm not sure how you go about that on iOS.

I haven't used Circle, but they have the corporate structure to be likely as trustworthy as any bank. Holding bitcoin you don't have to trust the currency creator (Fed Res, ECB, etc.) but you're still trusting someone else to hold and return your money when you want to use it.

Coinbase offers a multi-sig service that gives you control of the private keys, but that's not how their default wallet works.

Another option is a semi-online wallet service like blockchain.info. They keep an encrypted copy of your private keys in the cloud which makes the service really easy to use (their iphone app is pretty slick) but the keys are only decrypted on your device - giving you full ownership/control of your money - even if their service simply disappeared.

For some people online wallets like Coinbase and Circle will be more secure than managing the keys themselves. That being said if you're willing to take the time to learn how to secure the keys or a seed then you will be much more secure doing it yourself.

TL;DR: Sometimes. It depends on the technology behind the online wallet - not all have complete control of the private key.

Edit: @rossberry I'm not sure if you realize, but breadwallet is not an online wallet - it's about as full-featured and secure as you can get in a mobile wallet.
